searchText: Hi, I already shared this in <#745077610685661265> , also posting here for visibility, This is analysis based on the proposal to charge `350` gas for accessing individual code chunks (https://notes.ethereum.org/@vbuterin/code_chunk_gas_cost). The analysis shows how this would impact gas costs at block level, and also how this would impact transactions cost in for example, transactions calling the most gas-consuming contracts. You can see the analysis and results here: https://notes.ethereum.org/@ipsilon/code-chunk-cost-analysis <@!425343240212971521> Has anyone worked out how much this will actually slow down the EVM? <@!273808422753796097>'s description looks like a lot of per-instruction work, possibly worse that the 350 gas price per chunk, which is already a lot - do I correctly understand this to be adding over 10 gas to every executed instruction? <@!425274498732916736> and <@!211091239112671234> looked into the speed impact, see the implementations: https://github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/pull/22886 and https://github.com/ethereum/evmone/pull/326 Ok! Existing contracts wouldn't be able to make use of that, but it would be possible to change solidity to observe it. Exposing that to the users though I imagine would take a long time, as user-defined keys have been a contentious feature request since 2015. For non-looping code, yes Yes. Unless you loop or execute the same functions multiple times. But code that takes up a lot of gas pretty much has to be either loopring or SLOAD/SSTORE/precompile dominant In terms of performance, you need chunk index check in every instruction. Chunk size does not matter very much, but powers of two are better. @Pawel can the this be moved to the beginning of blocks, like gas and stack checking? <@!273808422753796097> I'm concerned about code that doesn't use (much) storage, but loops doing things like dense crypto computations. The EVM is often good enough for this purpose, and is getting better. If we add this much gas and overhead I fear we could lose pretty much all of our progress in that direction. What's the concern? That adding one array check per jump would break the efficiency? Ah yes, you should be able to do the chunk check once per jump/jumpdest/call, as between those ops access is predictable So at least the happy case ("already seen this code chunk") should be quite fast <@!273808422753796097> Looking at those implementations it looks to be a lot more work than one array check. And a lot of complexity. It's good if the work can be done once per block, but at present only evmone implements that optimization for gas and stack checks. I have an unfinished draft PR on that for turbogeth, which has already taken a non-trivial amount of work, and we don't know yet how effective it will be. Hmm why would that be the case In the EVM loop you would have an if statement: `if not accessed[pc//31]: ...` And in the already accessed case, you need to do nothing else Yes, but this is "chunk check once per instruction" not "per jump/jumpdest/call". <@!273808422753796097> For most instructions the additional geth code in the main loop is this: ``` if curChunk := uint16(pc / 31); codeChunkingActivated && curChunk != chunk { // Crossed to a new chunk here. Add cost if it hasn't already been // accessed if in.evm.StateDB.AddCodeChunkToAccessList(callContext.Contract.Address(), curChunk) { // Need to add to cost cost = 350 if !contract.UseGas(350) { return nil, ErrOutOfGas } } chunk = curChunk } ``` where `AddCodeChunkToAccessList` is non-trivial. For PUSH instructions (which are very common and cheap) we also run this code every time (not just every chunk): ``` if codeChunkingActivated && op >= PUSH1 && op <= PUSH32 { firstChunk := uint16((pc + 1) / 31) lastChunk := uint16((pc + 1 + uint64(op - PUSH1)) / 31) var pushdataCost uint64 for i := firstChunk; i <= lastChunk; i++ { if in.evm.StateDB.AddCodeChunkToAccessList(contract.Address(), i) { // Need to add to cost pushdataCost += 350 } } if !contract.UseGas(pushdataCost) { return nil, ErrOutOfGas } cost += pushdataCost } } ``` So the interpreter code becomes slower, more complex, and harder to understand and implement. And improving the speed makes the complexity of implementation even worse.

excerpts.author: hugo_delacruz
excerpts.content:
Hi, I already shared this in <#745077610685661265> , also posting here for visibility,
This is analysis based on the proposal to charge `350` gas for accessing
individual code chunks (https://notes.ethereum.org/@vbuterin/code_chunk_gas_cost).  The analysis shows how this would impact gas costs at block level, and also how this would impact transactions cost in for example, transactions calling the most gas-consuming contracts.

You can see the analysis and results here:

https://notes.ethereum.org/@ipsilon/code-chunk-cost-analysis

excerpts.author: gcolvin
excerpts.content: <@!425343240212971521>  Has anyone worked out how much this will actually slow down the EVM?  <@!273808422753796097>'s description looks like a lot of per-instruction work, possibly worse that the 350 gas price per chunk, which is already a lot - do I correctly understand this to be adding over 10 gas to every executed instruction?

excerpts.author: axic3354
excerpts.content: <@!425274498732916736> and <@!211091239112671234> looked into the speed impact, see the implementations: https://github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/pull/22886 and https://github.com/ethereum/evmone/pull/326

excerpts.author: axic3354
excerpts.content: Ok! Existing contracts wouldn't be able to make use of that, but it would be possible to change solidity to observe it. Exposing that to the users though I imagine would take a long time, as user-defined keys have been a contentious feature request since 2015.

excerpts.author: chfast
excerpts.content: Yes. Unless you loop or execute the same functions multiple times.

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: But code that takes up a lot of gas pretty much has to be either loopring or SLOAD/SSTORE/precompile dominant

excerpts.author: chfast
excerpts.content: In terms of performance, you need chunk index check in every instruction. Chunk size does not matter very much, but powers of two are better.

excerpts.content: @Pawel can the this be moved to the beginning of blocks, like gas and stack checking?

excerpts.author: gcolvin
excerpts.content: <@!273808422753796097> I'm concerned about code that doesn't use (much) storage, but loops doing things like dense crypto computations.  The EVM is often good enough for this purpose, and is getting better.  If we add this much gas and overhead I fear we could lose pretty much all of our progress in that direction.

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: What's the concern? That adding one array check per jump would break the efficiency?

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Ah yes, you should be able to do the chunk check once per jump/jumpdest/call, as between those ops access is predictable

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: So at least the happy case ("already seen this code chunk") should be quite fast

excerpts.author: gcolvin
excerpts.content: <@!273808422753796097>  Looking at those implementations it  looks to be a lot more work than one array check.  And a lot of complexity.  It's good if the work can be done once per block, but at present only evmone implements that optimization for gas and stack checks.  I have an unfinished draft PR on that for turbogeth, which has already taken a non-trivial amount of work, and we don't know yet how effective it will be.

excerpts.content: Yes, but this is "chunk check once per instruction" not "per jump/jumpdest/call".

excerpts.author: gcolvin
excerpts.content:
<@!273808422753796097> For most instructions the additional geth code in the main loop is this:

```
        if curChunk := uint16(pc / 31); codeChunkingActivated && curChunk != chunk {
            // Crossed to a new chunk here. Add cost if it hasn't already been
            // accessed
            if in.evm.StateDB.AddCodeChunkToAccessList(callContext.Contract.Address(), curChunk) {
                // Need to add to cost
                cost = 350
                if !contract.UseGas(350) {
                    return nil, ErrOutOfGas
                }
            }
            chunk = curChunk
        }
```
where `AddCodeChunkToAccessList` is non-trivial.  For PUSH instructions (which are very common and cheap) we also run this code every time (not just every chunk):
```
    if codeChunkingActivated &&  op >= PUSH1 && op <= PUSH32 {
            firstChunk := uint16((pc + 1) / 31)
            lastChunk := uint16((pc + 1 + uint64(op - PUSH1)) / 31)
            var pushdataCost uint64
            for i := firstChunk; i <= lastChunk; i++ {
                if in.evm.StateDB.AddCodeChunkToAccessList(contract.Address(), i) {
                    // Need to add to cost
                    pushdataCost += 350
                }
            }
            if !contract.UseGas(pushdataCost) {
                return nil, ErrOutOfGas
            }
            cost += pushdataCost
        }
    }
```
So the interpreter code becomes slower, more complex, and harder to understand and implement.  And improving the speed makes the complexity of implementation even worse.
